newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines seeks to avoid total APEC crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Philippines seeks to avoid total APEC crackdown.

text.p: The Philippines, proud of its reputation as Asia's most open democracy, is striving to avoid a crackdown on dissent such as occurred in Malaysia while guaranteeing the safety of heads of state at this month's APEC summit.

Security is paramount as the Philippines prepares to play host to U.S. President Bill Clinton, at least 15 other government leaders and several thousand delegates and journalists attending the November 25 Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
But President Fidel Ramos has said he is equally determined not to compromise the Philippines' strong democratic traditions, which have created the most open society in southeast Asia.
"We will provide maximum tolerance," he said recently.

Political analysts say the last thing the Manila goverment wants is something like the Kuala Lumpur debacle at the weekend when a youth group linked to Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition broke up a meeting about East Timor.

The Malaysian government disavowed any role in what delegates to the meeting, designed to draw attention to human rights violations in Indonesian-ruled East Timor, described as a frighteningly brutal assault.

Manila has already been accused of behaviour reminiscent of the dark days of former President Ferdinand Marcos's authoritarian rule in clearing away squatters from areas near venues for APEC meetings.
It also provoked protests when it banned Nobel Peace Prize laureate and East Timor independence leader Jose Ramos-Horta from attending anti-APEC meetings in Manila.

"On the one hand no chances are being taken but on the other, the government is going to allow all the counter-APEC activities to continue," said University of the Philippines political scientist Alex Magno.
The only exception will be banning some of the more prominent foreigners due to attend these conferences "to minimise the media attractiveness", Magno said.

Unlike most nations in the region, the Philippines has a free and lively press with newspapers routinely making outrageous allegations against public figures which would land them in jail in other countries or at least with hefty libel suits.

Refusing to heed the official line, Manila's press has splashed on its front pages news of fighting between the army and Moslem rebels on southern Basilan island, despite military attempts to restrict the release of information.

Apart from its press, the Philippines also has a vigorous network of political and social activists ever alert to the slightest encroachment on civil liberties, and ready to publicly and noisily protest against it.

Ironically, as Malaysia was deporting foreign activists who had come for the East Timor conference, Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim paid tribute to the Philippines' democratic principles in an article which appeared in a Manila newspaper on Sunday.

The Manila Chronicle article paid tribute to the Philippine revolt against Spanish rule 100 years ago, saying it was the first of its kind in Asia and "opened the floodgates of liberation from Western imperialism and proclaimed the dawn of the Asian renaissance".
It referred to the rekindling of this spirit when a peaceful popular revolt overthrew Marcos in 1986 and added:
"Democracy is a basic necessity ... yet some would have us believe that it is a luxury that Asians cannot afford," the article said.
